nodes.name: Probability of an event
nodes.statement: A probability P(A) is a number from 0 to 1. It gives the share of all equally weighted possibilities in which A happens.

nodes.name: Complement rule
nodes.statement: The probability that A does not happen is P(¬A) = 1 − P(A).

nodes.name: Joint probability
nodes.statement: P(A and B) is the probability that A and B both happen.

nodes.name: Conditional probability
nodes.statement: P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B). It is the share of B's cases in which A also happens.

nodes.name: Product rule
nodes.statement: Rearranging the definition gives P(A and B) = P(A|B)·P(B). By symmetry, the same joint probability also equals P(B|A)·P(A).

nodes.name: Bayes' theorem
nodes.statement: Setting the two forms of the product rule equal gives P(H|E) = P(E|H)·P(H) / P(E), for a hypothesis H and evidence E.

nodes.name: Prior probability
nodes.statement: The prior P(H) is the probability of hypothesis H before the evidence is seen.

nodes.name: Likelihood of evidence
nodes.statement: The likelihood P(E|H) is how probable the evidence E would be if H were true.

nodes.name: Posterior probability
nodes.statement: The posterior P(H|E) is the probability of H after the evidence E is taken into account.

nodes.name: Law of total probability
nodes.statement: Because H and ¬H cover every case, P(E) = P(E|H)·P(H) + P(E|¬H)·P(¬H).

nodes.name: Evidence as normalizer
nodes.statement: P(E) has the same value whichever hypothesis is being scored. It only rescales the posteriors so that they sum to 1.

nodes.name: Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior
nodes.statement: Up to that shared constant, the posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior, P(H|E) ∝ P(E|H)·P(H).

nodes.name: P(A|B) differs from P(B|A)
nodes.statement: The two conditionals divide the same joint probability by different totals, P(B) and P(A). So they are equal only when P(A) = P(B).

nodes.name: Base rate
nodes.statement: The base rate is how common a condition is in the group being tested, such as 1% of people having a disease. It serves as the prior.

nodes.name: Sensitivity and false positives
nodes.statement: A test's sensitivity is P(positive|sick). Its false positive rate is P(positive|healthy).

nodes.name: Rare disease example
nodes.statement: With a 1% base rate, 90% sensitivity and a 9% false positive rate, P(sick|positive) = 0.009 / (0.009 + 0.0891). That is only about 9%.

nodes.name: Natural frequencies
nodes.statement: Out of 1000 people, 10 are sick and 9 of them test positive, while about 89 of the 990 healthy people also test positive. So only 9 of about 98 positive results belong to sick people.

nodes.name: Base rate neglect
nodes.statement: Judging P(sick|positive) by the test's accuracy alone confuses it with P(positive|sick). This error ignores the prior and badly overstates the risk when the condition is rare.

nodes.name: Odds of a hypothesis
nodes.statement: The odds of H are P(H) / P(¬H). A probability of 0.2 corresponds to odds of 1 to 4.

nodes.name: Likelihood ratio
nodes.statement: The likelihood ratio P(E|H) / P(E|¬H) says how many times more probable the evidence is under H than under ¬H.

nodes.name: Odds form of Bayes
nodes.statement: Dividing Bayes' theorem for H by Bayes' theorem for ¬H cancels P(E). What remains is posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio.

nodes.name: Updating in sequence
nodes.statement: When pieces of evidence are independent given each hypothesis, the posterior after one piece serves as the prior for the next. The order in which they arrive does not change the final result.

nodes.name: Evidence adds in log-odds
nodes.statement: Taking logarithms turns the odds form into a sum. Each independent piece of evidence then adds its own log likelihood ratio.

nodes.name: Second positive test
nodes.statement: In the disease example, the likelihood ratio of a positive result is 0.9 / 0.09 = 10. A second independent positive test turns odds of about 1 to 10 into about 1 to 1, a probability near 50%.

nodes.name: Certain priors never move
nodes.statement: A prior of exactly 0 stays 0 under any evidence, because Bayes' rule multiplies the prior by the likelihood. A prior of 1 stays 1 for the same reason applied to ¬H.

nodes.name: Evidence needs a contrast
nodes.statement: Evidence changes belief only when it is more probable under one hypothesis than under the other. A likelihood ratio of exactly 1 leaves the odds unchanged.
